content: Dystocia, which is the opposite of eutocia, refers to an abnormal or difficult childbirth or labor. This condition can occur due to several factors, including uncoordinated uterine contractions, an abnormal position or presentation of the fetus, or a mismatch between the size of the fetal head and the maternal pelvis, known as cephalopelvic disproportion. In cases of uncoordinated uterine activity, oxytocin is frequently administered to stimulate effective contractions. However, pregnancies complicated by dystocia often require assisted delivery methods, such as the use of forceps, vacuum extraction (ventouse), or, more commonly, cesarean section. Dystocia is associated with several significant risks, including fetal death, respiratory depression, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (a type of brain injury caused by oxygen deprivation), and brachial nerve injury. A specific form of dystocia, known as shoulder dystocia, occurs when the infant's anterior shoulder becomes lodged behind the maternal pubic symphysis, necessitating considerable manipulation to allow the shoulder to pass. Another type of dystocia is characterized by a prolonged second stage of labor, which is defined as the failure to deliver the fetus within three hours after the cervix has fully dilated. Dystocia is also referred to by other terms, including difficult labor, abnormal labor, difficult childbirth, abnormal childbirth, and dysfunctional labor. In birds and reptiles, dystocia is referred to as egg binding, a condition in which the animal is unable to pass an egg.
